items.content:
AMD to Report Fiscal Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD to Report Fiscal Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results
October 06, 2026 4:15 pm EDT
Download as PDF
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Oct.  06, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) announced today that it will report fiscal third quarter 2026 financial results on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, after the market close. Management will conduct a conference call to discuss these results at 5 p.m. ET / 2 p.m. PT. Interested parties are invited to listen to the webcast of the conference call via AMD’s Investor Relations website:
ir.amd.com
.
AMD also announced it will participate in the following events with the financial community:
UBS Global Technology and AI Conference on Tuesday, Dec. 1, 2026.
Barclays 24
th
Annual Global Technology Conference on Wednesday, Dec. 9, 2026.
Webcasts of the presentations can be accessed on AMD’s Investor Relations website:
ir.amd.com
.
About AMD
AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) drives innovation in high-performance and AI computing to solve the world’s most important challenges. Today, AMD technology powers billions of experiences across cloud and AI infrastructure, embedded systems, AI PCs and gaming. With a broad portfolio of AI-optimized CPUs, GPUs, networking and software, AMD delivers full-stack AI solutions that provide the performance and scalability needed for a new era of intelligent computing. Learn more at
www.amd.com
.

Expanding our support for scientists
View more
We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our
AI for Science program
, which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.
We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted
Team plan for scientists
and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)
Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.
Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with
HHMI Janelia Research Campus
to develop the
Model Hardware Standard
(MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the
Allen Institute
, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.
AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.
Science funders and societies
Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:
The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation.
Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.
The Simons Foundation.
This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.
Schmidt Sciences.
Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.
Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy.
This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.
The US National Science Foundation.
This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.
CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society.
For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.
Institutions
Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:
Space Telescope Science Institute.
STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.
Wellcome Sanger Institute.
One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.
The Francis Crick Institute.
Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.
Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences.
One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.
EMBL.
The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.
Gladstone Institutes.
An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.
Research projects and initiatives
As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:
FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience).
It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.
LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system).
Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.
AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research).
Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.
gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease).
The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.
Tau Ceti (mathematics).
This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.
Centre for Population Genomics.
A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.
What’s next
Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.
As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

Diagnose Distributed AI Workload Failures with NVIDIA Attribution
Use this open-source tool to correlate workload-scoped logs, metrics, and scheduler state into a reproducible diagnosis on your own cluster.
Nov 02, 2026
By
Gargi Prasad
,
Jason Sewall
,
Aaron Blakeman
,

and

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA Attribution correlates workload-scoped logs, metrics, telemetry, and scheduler state to produce a structured diagnosis with outcome, root cause, affected nodes, supporting symptoms, and an evidence trail.
The system operates through two deployable components: the Attribution Service, which exposes a REST API for the core attribution engine, and the Attribution Blueprint, a Python reference orchestrator that connects cluster schedulers and telemetry sources to the Service.
The Blueprint ships with execution-context connectors for
Slurm
, Kueue, and static inputs, plus log and metric connectors for Loki, local files, Kubernetes pod logs, and PromQL metrics.
In production across NVIDIA AI infrastructure, the system analyzes millions of workloads weekly across hundreds of thousands of GPUs and has identified fabric failure patterns around specific host and switch ports.
The attribution process follows four stages: scoping the workload, collecting observations, extracting and correlating events through deterministic rules, and returning a structured result with terminal state and attributed domain.
A worked example demonstrates how an NVLink signal integrity issue on one node is identified as the root cause while downstream NCCL errors across ranks are preserved as supporting symptoms.
Next Steps
Clone the
NVIDIA Attribution repository
to access the source code and sample workloads.
Follow the
quickstart
to run the sample workflow and inspect diagnoses in the local dashboard.
Review the
Blueprint configuration reference
to connect your own scheduler and telemetry backends.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
In distributed AI workloads, a single error can produce a cascade of symptoms. A GPU or fabric event may surface as NCCL errors on other ranks, scheduler state changes, and thousands of downstream messages. The reported exception shows where the workload stopped, not where the failure began.
In this post, you’ll learn how to run NVIDIA Attribution on sample workload evidence, inspect the diagnosis, and explore how attribution rules identify failure patterns.
NVIDIA Attribution correlates workload-scoped logs, metrics, telemetry, and scheduler state and returns a structured diagnosis: outcome, root cause, affected nodes, supporting symptoms, and evidence trail. Workload-centric means analyzing failures in the context of a workload rather than as isolated node events. Deterministic rules make the results reproducible and customizable, while structured output enables integration with existing health and recovery systems.
NVIDIA health and resilience software helps teams keep AI workloads running. NVIDIA Attribution explains why a workload failed and provides evidence to guide the next action. It complements readiness checks, continuous health monitoring, and the systems that repair infrastructure and restart workloads.
NVIDIA Attribution
, the workload-centric failure-attribution system used across NVIDIA AI infrastructure, is open source.
Used in production across NVIDIA AI infrastructure for years, NVIDIA Attribution analyzes millions of workloads each week across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. In one large RDMA-backed cluster, it correlated port errors, connection resets, and scheduler events to identify patterns around specific host and switch ports, helping teams target fabric repairs and congestion tuning.
It includes two deployable components: the NVIDIA Attribution Service and the NVIDIA Attribution Blueprint; both components utilize a core attribution engine. The Service makes attribution available through a RESTAPI; the Blueprint connects cluster schedulers and telemetry sources to the Service and writes the result.
Turn workload evidence into one diagnosis
NVIDIA Attribution Service analyzes one workload attempt at a time. The Blueprint gathers the workload context and evidence, the Service extracts and correlates events, and the Blueprint returns a structured result.
The path has four stages:
Scope the workload.
The Blueprint identifies the workload attempt from scheduler identifiers or from an explicit execution window and node allocation.
Collect observations.
Log and metric connectors produce workload-scoped
Observation
records from application logs, syslogs, GPU driver and Fabric Manager messages, scheduler history, node and network metrics.
Extract and correlate events.
The Service invokes the attribution engine to identify significant events such as GPU XIDs, NCCL failures, scheduler transitions, and metric conditions. Deterministic rules evaluate their timing and interaction, separate downstream symptoms from the event that caused the failure, and identify the root cause.
Return a structured result.
The Blueprint combines the verdict with the workload outcome (
terminal_state
), attributed domain (
sub_domain
), symptoms, affected nodes, and a record of collector coverage and errors.
From applogs to attribution
What follows is a worked example of extracting evidence, interpreting events, and preserving the symptoms that explain a distributed workload failure.
Consider a multi-rank training workload in which one GPU encounters a hard fault e.g:
XID 149
and NCCL errors follow across other ranks. NVIDIA Attribution correlates events across nodes, identifies the XID as the root cause, retains the NCCL failures in the symptom chain, and names the responsible node. The workload is reported as a hardware failure rather than a set of independent communication errors.
A failed collective can leave error reports on several nodes. Those reports tell us where the workload noticed a problem. To explain the failure, NVIDIA Attribution combines them with evidence from other sources and evaluates the symptoms together.
In this synthetic workload, application logs contain three different NCCL errors. System logs on node-02 contain XID 149 with error words that decode to NVLink signal integrity issue. We will follow that evidence through the rules pipeline.
Interpreting logs with extraction
The Extraction phase is the first to run; it runs on the raw input logs and produces structured events to be processed by later stages.
Figure 1. Extraction turns application and system logs into typed events with source provenance. These will be processed by later phases in the attribution process
Decode NVLink evidence during filtering
Filter rules read and write the event stream. The EARLY-stage
HandleXidBurstEvents
rule reads the XID burst evidence, decodes the error words, and emits an attribution event for signal integrity issue on
node-02
. The three NCCL events remain unchanged during this step.
Figure 2. EARLY filtering decodes NVLink signal integrity issue while leaving the three NCCL events unchanged
Figure 2, above, The figure abbreviates the decoded symptom as XID-149.4 signal integrity issue. The filter also emits parser information for inspection.
Refine the symptoms into one attribution
The framework materializes events into per-node symptoms, runs per-node scrubbing, and aggregates the surviving symptoms into a job-wide set. In this example, all four candidates reach FINAL refinement.
Xid149AndNvlinkFiltering
retains the signal integrity symptom and demotes the other node symptoms.
Gb200PriorityRootCause
reduces the active job-wide symptom set. Outcome mapping then produces the hardware-failure attribution.
Figure 3. FINAL refinement surfaces signal integrity issue on node-02 and retains the NCCL reports as interesting evidence
The attribution surfaces
node-02
and signal integrity issue. The NCCL reports remain useful evidence: demotion preserves their original sources as “interesting,” so they can still be inspected.
When multiple causes fit the evidence,
sub_domain
is ambiguous. Quality of attribution is dependent on the quality and completeness of the underlying telemetry. The diagnosis records that distinction, correctly reflecting uncertainty instead of converting incomplete evidence into a definitive diagnosis.
Service and Blueprint architecture
Figure 4. NVIDIA Attribution Service and Blueprint architecture diagram showing how the Attribution Blueprint collects workload evidence from scheduler and telemetry sources, passes it to the Attribution Service for analysis, and writes a structured diagnosis to output sinks including a read-only dashboard
The attribution engine contains the rules engine and core attribution logic. The Attribution Service exposes that logic through an HTTP API, and the Blueprint handles cluster-specific integration. This separation lets teams apply the same attribution logic across clusters while adapting scheduler, telemetry, and output connectors to each environment.
Attribution Service:
A self-hosted HTTP wrapper around the core attribution engine that receives normalized observations and returns one verdict for each workload.
Attribution Blueprint:
A Python reference orchestrator that discovers workloads, resolves the
ExecutionContext
, runs collectors, calls the Service, enriches the verdict, writes the
AttributionBlueprintResult
, and supplies a read-only dashboard. This is intended to be a reference implementation for practitioners to customize the solution to their environment.
The Blueprint ships with:
Execution-context connectors for
Slurm
,
Kueue
, and static inputs
Log and metric connectors for
Loki
, local files, Kubernetes pod logs, and
PromQL
metrics
Output connectors for stdout and SQLite
Blueprints can run near each cluster’s data sources, with either a dedicated Attribution Service for each Blueprint or a shared Service for multiple Blueprints. There is flexibility on how you want to customize your deployment, e.g: one to one or one to many. Downstream systems consume
terminal_state
and
sub_domain
instead of parsing product-specific logs.
Extending Attribution to your infrastructure
Open sourcing NVIDIA Attribution enables infrastructure teams to encode a failure pattern once and apply it across workloads and clusters. Developers can add rules for new failure modes, implement connectors for their schedulers and telemetry backends, and route
AttributionBlueprintResult
records into incident, recovery, and fleet-management systems. Because extensions use the same
ExecutionContext
,
Observation
, and result contracts, new integrations feed the same diagnosis pipeline.
Walkthrough
The earlier example illustrates how a GPU fault can lead to NCCL errors across ranks. In this walkthrough, you’ll use NVIDIA Attribution to analyze NVLink error evidence from a recorded training workload. You’ll run the included sample, inspect the diagnosis and source evidence, and examine the rule that narrows the reported symptoms. You’ll then use the NVIDIA recovery guidance to identify the next action for the affected node.
The walkthrough uses two components:
The Attribution Service runs the analysis rules.
The Attribution Blueprint reads the workload context and logs, calls the Service, and stores the result for inspection in a local dashboard.
The sample evidence ships with the repository, so you can follow the analysis before connecting a live cluster.
Run the sample workflow
The NVIDIA Attribution
quickstart
builds the Attribution Service and dashboard in Docker, then uses the Blueprint to process sample workload evidence committed to the repository. You need Docker and the
uv
package manager.
Clone the repository and run the sample workflow:
git clone https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/attribution.git nvidia-attribution
cd nvidia-attribution
docker build \
-f blueprint/docker/Dockerfile \
-t attribution-blueprint-web:quickstart \
"$PWD"
mkdir -p .attribution-sample
docker run -d --rm \
--name attribution-blueprint-web-local \
-e ATTRIBUTION_DB=/data/attributions.db \
-p "127.0.0.1:8000:8000" \
-p "127.0.0.1:8080:8080" \
-v "$PWD/.attribution-sample:/data" \
attribution-blueprint-web:quickstart
uv run --project blueprint --frozen nvidia-attribution-blueprint \
--configs blueprint/examples/static/configs \
--connector attribution service_url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
--connector output db sqlite path .attribution-sample/attributions.db
Open
http://127.0.0.1:8080
to inspect each workload’s diagnosis, affected nodes, supporting symptoms, and evidence trail.
The rules engine uses checked-in declarative and Python rules. This production rule recognizes an invalid Pyxis argument in an application log and includes a co-located test case:
[[extractor]]
name     = "SrunInvalidPyxisArgument"
match_re = "srun: error: Invalid --(?:no-)?container-\\S+ argument:"
emit     = { type = "bad_node", symptom = "srun: invalid pyxis argument" }
[[extractor.cases]]
expect  = "bad"
line    = "srun: error: Invalid --container-mounts argument: /nonexistent"
symptom = "srun: invalid pyxis argument"
At startup, the Service loads the bundled rule catalog and evaluates the inline cases. A rule change is committed and shipped with the Service; rules are not uploaded dynamically through the HTTP API. The repository’s
rule-authoring guide
explains how to select the appropriate rule form, register new symptoms, add tests, and verify the complete catalog.
Get started
Clone the
NVIDIA Attribution repository
and follow the
quickstart
to run the sample and inspect its diagnoses. To use Attribution with your own infrastructure, see the
Blueprint configuration reference
for scheduler and telemetry connectors, and learn how to
add an extractor rule
for new evidence patterns.

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA Recovery
automates workload-level recovery across a cluster's training jobs around the clock, detecting interruptions through application logs, GPU metrics, and scheduler signals.
The service coordinates a four-stage recovery loop that detects anomalies, attributes failures, isolates implicated nodes, and restarts or stops workloads based on configured policy.
Integration with Slurm uses a reference Advisor Controller deployable via Helm chart in either in-cluster or SSH mode, keeping the recovery service independent of scheduler internals.
New deployments start in monitor mode by default, publishing recovery recommendations without taking scheduler actions so operators can validate signal quality before enabling autonomous recovery.
A persistent audit trail records every detection pattern, action taken, timestamp, workload identifier, and attribution verdict, with the Recovery Console providing a live operator dashboard across scheduler types.
Production monitoring on one training cluster from July 9 to October 9 covered nearly 200 jobs per day and recorded approximately 8,550 anomaly detections with mean detection and recovery-action latencies of 69 and 94 seconds respectively.
Next Steps
Clone the
dsx-ai-factory/NVIDIA-Recovery
repository to access the source code and issue tracker.
Run the quickstart guide to deploy NVIDIA Recovery locally without a physical GPU.
Review the operator deployment guide for in-cluster and SSH-based Slurm deployment instructions.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
As distributed AI training scales, failures across hardware and software dependencies increasingly disrupt training progress, making fast, reliable recovery essential. A stalled training rank can trigger an NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) timeout, a GPU node can stop responding to the scheduler, or a straggler can slow the entire job. Each disruption is manageable on its own, but the cumulative impact and recovery overhead determine how efficiently the system converts wall-clock time into productive training progress or
goodput
.
Manual recovery becomes unsustainable when it must cover every training job across a cluster, around the clock, at scale. Each interruption demands log analysis, fault isolation, and a restart from a saved checkpoint, while affected GPUs remain idle during recovery. As the number and size of training jobs grow, overlapping failures increase the engineering burden and wasted GPU-hours. Without continuous coverage, those losses can accumulate, increasing overall compute costs and extending time to train.
NVIDIA Recovery
, part of
NVIDIA DSX OS
, the modular software portfolio with the
NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform
, is an open-source, workload-level service that automates recovery across a cluster’s training jobs, around the clock. It detects interruptions using application logs, GPU metrics, and scheduler signals, uses failure attribution to identify implicated resources, and coordinates isolation and checkpoint restarts from checkpoints on healthy capacity. By automating this recovery loop across workloads, it handles concurrent interruptions, reduces manual intervention, and helps sustain training goodput. This post explains how the recovery loop works, how NVIDIA Recovery integrates with
Slurm
, and how to deploy it on your own cluster.
Workload recovery is a distinct AI factory concern
Our previous
NVIDIA DGX Cloud resilience post
,
GTC talk
and
NVIDIA Mission Control 2.5 post
describe a layered approach to keeping training productive. NVIDIA Recovery builds on that architecture by connecting infrastructure remediation to workload recovery.
Break-fix automation identifies faulty nodes, removes them from service, and routes hardware for remediation. Framework-level libraries such as
NVRx
provide recovery, hang detection, and straggler mitigation within individual training jobs, but each user must configure and manage these capabilities for their own workloads. Cluster workload managers such as Slurm manage resource allocation, queuing, and container execution.
Workload recovery is a distinct coordination problem: restoring productive training requires attributing failures to their causes, deciding whether and where affected jobs should restart, and acting consistently across workloads that share infrastructure. Addressing this problem requires a cluster-level control loop that integrates infrastructure remediation, framework-level recovery, and cluster workload management, with operational metrics that track recovery latency, recovery success rate, and time to restore productive training.
Multi-level NVIDIA health and resilience stack
As shown in Figure 1, below, NVIDIA Recovery provides the dedicated workload recovery layer within the
DSX OS Stack
. Node health monitoring and isolation depend on the cluster’s orchestration and workload management stack. Kubernetes deployments use
NVSentinel
to monitor GPU health metrics and
XID
events and automatically cordon and drain faulty nodes. Many Slurm sites check node health with custom prolog and epilog scripts. The slurm-operator from the
Slinky
project natively supports and injects these same scripts when running Slurm on Kubernetes. Within individual training jobs, NVRx provides a library for in-job recovery and hang detection. NVIDIA Recovery coordinates recovery
across workloads at the cluster level
, integrating with these capabilities to manage job restarts, placement, and node exclusion.
Figure 1. NVIDIA Recovery’s role in health and resilience integration
These layers operate independently without hard dependencies, allowing you to adopt each modular component or plug in your own platform component to integrate. For example, if your cluster already relies on NVSentinel or NVIDIA Health Validation, you can integrate NVIDIA Recovery with little or no changes to your existing health workflows.
For environments already running NVRx, NVIDIA Recovery fills the gap that in-job restart cannot reach by managing the cross-workload lifecycle and node exclusion. When paired with NVIDIA Attribution, it receives rich cross-layer diagnostic verdicts that enrich the persistent audit trail.
Cost of the gap
At cluster scale, rare per-GPU failures compound. Even if each GPU operates without failure on a given day with 99.9% probability, a job spanning 10,000 GPUs completes that day uninterrupted with a probability of only
0.999
10,000
≈ 0.005%. This explains why, in
an 11-month study of 24,000 A100 GPUs at Meta
, hardware failures interrupted fewer than 1% of jobs while those jobs accounted for 19% of GPU runtime: the largest, longest-running jobs are the most exposed.
NVIDIA Recovery automates recovery across a cluster’s training workloads, and is useful for both small and large distributed runs. Across many smaller jobs, interruptions accumulate, increasing the operational burden. In large jobs, each interruption affects more GPUs, amplifying the compute cost of recovery. Automated recovery addresses both challenges.
Our production observations underscore the need for such efficient, automated recovery that scales across cluster workloads: from July 9 to Oct. 9, NVIDIA Recovery monitoring on one training cluster covered nearly 200 jobs per day and recorded approximately 8,550 anomaly detections, with mean detection and recovery-action latencies of 69 and 94 seconds, respectively. This unattended, cluster-wide response reduces dependence on individual engineers and per-user recovery arrangements as interruptions accumulate. Recovery-action latency ends at the automated action; scheduling and checkpoint restoration determine when productive training resumes.
The automated recovery loop
NVIDIA Recovery coordinates recovery across the cluster’s training workloads. Four stages organize the loop, with actions determined by the interruption and configured policy:
Detect
: The Anomaly Detector combines application logs and scheduler signals to identify crashes, hangs, and stragglers. It recognizes PyTorch and NCCL failures, CUDA errors, and interconnect failure patterns. Missing progress signals or recognized communication-hang patterns indicate potential hangs; sustained throughput degradation relative to a recent baseline indicates potential stragglers.
Attribute
: NVIDIA Recovery uses the scheduler signals and application logs gathered during detection to classify the interruption and guide recovery actions. Optional integration with NVIDIA Attribution adds deeper diagnosis to distinguish hardware faults, system-software issues, and application bugs. This evidence informs node exclusion and enriches the audit trail. Operators can also integrate their own attribution service and adopt NVIDIA Recovery independently.
Isolate:
The Anomaly Remediator applies the recovery recommendation, excluding implicated nodes from subsequent restart attempts or stopping the workload when further retries would be unproductive. It tracks implicated nodes across attempts to avoid recurring failures. In addition, a safety net (watchdog service) allows normal scheduling to proceed if a recovery decision takes too long or outright fails, preventing workloads from waiting indefinitely.
Restart or Stop
: The scheduler integration acts on NVIDIA Recovery’s recommendation through the Advisor API to restart the workload or stop unproductive retries. On restart, the application resumes from its last saved checkpoint using its existing restart logic. If the job fails to save a new checkpoint across a configurable number of attempts, further retries can be stopped. The audit trail records restart and stop decisions, with allocation restart, restored training progress, and training completion tracked as distinct events.
Figure 2. NVIDIA Recovery’s automated recovery loop
NVIDIA Recovery integration with workload schedulers
NVIDIA Recovery runs as a control-plane service and communicates with the cluster’s scheduler integration through an HTTP or gRPC API. It supports Slurm, with Kubernetes support on the roadmap. Recovery recommendations follow a common API contract, which a cluster-side controller translates into actions for the workload manager. This keeps NVIDIA Recovery independent of scheduler internals and avoids changes to application code.
For Slurm, the reference Advisor Controller is available for easy deployment as a Helm chart. It supports two modes: 1) In-cluster mode where the controller runs within the cluster; 2) SSH mode where the control plane connects to Slurm remotely, without adding an in-cluster service. This provides an option when deploying a new cluster component requires a change window or security review.
NVIDIA Recovery records each recovery recommendation before the controller acts, creating an audit trail of intended actions. If the controller restarts during recovery, it checks the current scheduler state before proceeding, a safeguard against repeating actions already completed.
Running it: Monitor mode and the audit trail
New deployments start in monitor mode by default. In this mode, NVIDIA Recovery publishes advice and records what it would have done, and it takes no scheduler actions. Review that advice, compare the decisions with what your own engineers would have done, and switch to action mode per cluster once you are satisfied with the signal-to-noise ratio.
controller:
environment: prod
acknowledgeSchedulerActions: false
watchdog:
enabled: true
mode: observe
acknowledgeSchedulerActions: false
environmentPattern: prod
IBM Research took this path on their Slurm cluster. They ran in monitor mode first, compared the advice with their own manual recovery decisions, and enabled autonomous action after validating the signal. Verda, a neocloud provider, deployed on Victoria Logs rather than Loki and collaborated on a VictoriaLogs connector for the repository, jump starting the OSS partner program.
NVIDIA Recovery writes each action to a persistent, queryable audit trail. Each entry captures the matched detection pattern, the action taken (kill, requeue, release, or node exclusion), the timestamp, the workload identifier, and the NVIDIA Attribution verdict when one was returned. Policy-engine actions and watchdog actions land in the same trail, so the record has no gaps.
The Recovery Console is the operator dashboard. It shows live workload state across scheduler types, surfaces anomaly flags inline, and gives you a per-workload timeline of every detection event and recovery action.
Video 1. A walkthrough of NVIDIA Recovery with Slurm on Kubernetes, from environment setup and job configuration to a job failure, automatic recovery, and attribution
NVIDIA Recovery is available in the
dsx-ai-factory/NVIDIA-Recovery
GitHub repo under the Apache 2.0 license. Getting a first workload under recovery takes three steps:
Install the chart. NVIDIA Recovery deploys from a single Helm umbrella chart. A bundled MySQL sub-chart ships with it so you can run the quickstart locally without provisioning a database or a physical GPU. For production, point the chart at a managed MySQL service. The operator deployment guide in the repository covers both paths and the current version requirements for Kubernetes, Helm, and Slurm.
Validate your signals. Point the chart at your existing Loki or Victoria Logs endpoint and your Prometheus scrape target, then run the log ingestion configurator before your first workload. It tests your signals against the NVIDIA Recovery contract, maps label names that differ from the defaults, and surfaces mismatches before they become silent failures.
Opt a workload in. Add one directive to your sbatch submission script:
#SBATCH --comment='{"nvidia-recovery":{"environment":"prod","mode":"observe"}}'
From there, NVIDIA Recovery monitors the workload through application logs and scheduler signals. In monitor mode, it publishes recovery recommendations without taking action. After validating those recommendations in the Recovery Console, enable autonomous recovery by setting mode to action and acknowledgeSchedulerActions to true in the Helm values.
Additional resources cover the rest:
The dsx-ai-factory/nvidia-recovery GitHub repo, for the source and the issue tracker.
The quickstart guide, which runs without a physical GPU.
The operator deployment guide, for in-cluster and SSH-based Slurm deployments.
The architecture reference, for how the control plane fits together.
NVIDIA Attribution
is the recommended companion deployment. It gives NVIDIA Recovery a deeper diagnostic verdict and a richer audit trail; it is optional, and it ships alongside NVIDIA Recovery.
What Comes Next
This Version recovers Slurm jobs, including Slurm on Kubernetes through slurm-operator. Two capabilities come next. Recovery for Slurm job arrays gives the hyperparameter sweeps many teams run as arrays the same protection as single jobs: each failed task is recovered on its own, and Recovery stops when failures look systemic. Native Kubernetes recovery starts with JobSet and Kubeflow PyTorchJob, using the open-source
Workload Map
project to support each workload type.
Beyond those, the
roadmap
covers sharper failure classification, a clearer record of every recovery decision in the dashboard and the API so you can feed it into your own observability tools, and the work toward a stable release. Upvote and comment on roadmap issues to shape what comes first.
IBM Research has deployed NVIDIA Recovery for training workloads and is working with the team on refining failure patterns from them. Verda, the first NVIDIA Cloud Partner to deploy it, runs NVIDIA Recovery with VictoriaLogs and has submitted its first pull requests. As more adopters contribute, their changes go through the same review as NVIDIA’s own.
NVIDIA Recovery is part of DSX OS, NVIDIA’s open-source software layer for AI factory operations. It is licensed under Apache 2.0.
Get started
NVIDIA Recovery automates the recovery cycle that manual processes leave to an engineer at 3 a.m. Clone the repository, run the configurator against your telemetry stack, and opt a workload in. The first interruption will show you what the loop looks like end to end.

This procedure covers upgrading from Apigee hybrid
version 1.15.x to Apigee hybrid version 1.16.13 and
from previous releases of hybrid 1.16.x to version
1.16.13.
Use the same procedures for minor version upgrades (for example version 1.15
to 1.16) and for patch release upgrades (for example
1.16.0 to 1.16.13).
If you are upgrading from Apigee hybrid version 1.14 or older, you must first upgrade to
hybrid version 1.15 before upgrading to version 1.16.13.
See the instructions for
Upgrading
Apigee hybrid to version 1.15
.
Changes from Apigee hybrid v1.15
Please note the following changes:
Seccomp profiles
:
Starting in
version 1.16
,
Apigee hybrid now offers the capability to apply Seccomp Profiles to your runtime components,
significantly enhancing the security posture of your deployment. This feature allows Apigee
administrators and security teams to restrict the system calls a containerized process can make
to the host's kernel. By limiting a container to only the necessary syscalls, you can:
Enhance Security: Mitigate the risk of container breakouts and privilege escalation.
Enforce Least Privilege: Ensure components only have access to the exact system calls
required for their operation.
Meet Compliance: Provide a critical control for meeting stringent security compliance
requirements.
For more information, see
Configure Seccomp profiles for
pod security
.
UDCA in Apigee hybrid removal
:
In Apigee hybrid
version 1.16
,
the Unified Data Collection Agent (UDCA) component has been removed. The responsibilities of
sending analytics, trace, and deployment status data to the Apigee control plane are now handled
using a
Google Cloud Pub/Sub
based data pipeline. Using the Pub/Sub
based data pipeline has been the default data collection mechanism since Apigee hybrid
version 1.14.0
.
apigee-guardrails
service account
:
In v1.16.0, Apigee Hybrid introduces an
apigee-guardrails
Google IAM service account. This is used by the
apigee-operator
chart during installation to check that all needed APIs are enabled in your project.
See:
Diagnosing issues with guardrails
About service accounts:
apigee-guardrails
create-service-account
Installation Part 2: Step 4: Create service accounts
Installation Part 2: Step 5: Set up service account authentication
Support for cert-manager release 1.18 and 1.19
:
Apigee hybrid v1.16 supports cert-manager
release 1.18
and
release 1.19
. In cert-manager release 1.18, there is a change to the default value of
Certificate.Spec.PrivateKey.rotationPolicy
that can impact traffic. If you are upgrading from a previous version of Apigee hybrid, and you are uprading to cert-manager release 1.18 or above, follow the
Upgrade cert-manager
prodedure in this guide.
Note:
This does not affect fresh installations of Apigee hybrid v1.6.
For additional information about features in Hybrid version 1.16, see the
Apigee hybrid
v1.16.13 release notes
.
Prerequisites
Before upgrading to hybrid version 1.16, make sure your
installation meets the following requirements:
If your hybrid installation is running a version older than v1.15, you
must upgrade to version 1.15 before upgrading to v1.16.
See
Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version 1.15
.
Helm version v3.14.2+.
kubectl
: A supported version of
kubectl
appropriate for your Kubernetes platform version. See
Supported platforms and versions:
kubectl
.
cert-manager: A supported version of cert-manager. See
Supported platforms and versions: cert-manager
. If needed, you will upgrade cert-manager in the
Prepare to upgrade to version 1.16
section below.
Before you upgrade to 1.16.13 - limitations and important notes
Apigee hybrid 1.16.13 introduces a new enhanced per-environment
proxy limit that lets you deploy more proxies and shared flows in a single
environment.  See
Limits: API Proxies
to understand the limits on the number of proxies and shared flows you may deploy per
environment.  This feature is available only on newly created hybrid organizations,
and cannot be applied to upgraded orgs. To use this feature, perform a fresh
installation of hybrid 1.16.13, and create a new organization.
This feature is available exclusively as part of the
2024 subscription plan
,
and is subject to the entitlements granted under that subscription. See
Enhanced per-environment proxy limits
to learn more about this feature.
Upgrading to Apigee hybrid version 1.16 may require
downtime.
When upgrading the Apigee controller to version 1.16.13, all Apigee
deployments undergo a rolling restart. To minimize downtime in production hybrid environments
during a rolling restart, make sure you are running at least two clusters (in the same or
different region/data center). Divert all production traffic to a single cluster and take the
cluster you are about to upgrade offline, and then proceed with the upgrade process. Repeat
the process for each cluster.
Apigee recommends that once you begin the upgrade, you should upgrade all clusters as soon as possible to reduce the chances
of production impact. There is no time limit on when all remaining clusters must be upgraded
after the first one is upgraded. However, until all remaining clusters are upgraded Cassandra
backup and restore cannot work with mixed versions. For example, a backup from Hybrid
1.15 cannot be used to restore a Hybrid 1.16
instance.
Management plane changes do not need to be fully suspended during an upgrade.
Any required temporary suspensions to management plane changes are noted in the upgrade
instructions below.
Upgrading to version 1.16.13 overview
The procedures for upgrading Apigee hybrid are organized in the following sections:
Prepare to upgrade
.
Install hybrid runtime version 1.16.13
.
Prepare to upgrade to version 1.16
Back up your hybrid installation
These instructions use the environment variable
APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
for the directory
in your file system where you have installed the Helm charts. If needed, change directory
into this directory and define the variable with the following command:
Linux
export APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME=$PWD
echo
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
Mac OS
export APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME=$PWD
echo
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
Windows
set APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME=%CD%
echo %APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME%
Make a backup copy of your version 1.15
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME/
directory. You can use any backup process. For example,
you can create a
tar
file of your entire directory with:
tar -czvf
$APIGEE_HELM_CHARTS_HOME
/../apigee-helm-charts-v1.15-backup.tar.gz

items.title: Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents See Google A2Ui in action! Learn how to natively render agentic UIs across Langchain, AWS Strands, Microsoft agents, and Goog
items.content:
Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents
- Google Developers Blog
Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents
OCT. 29, 2026
Google A2UI Team
Atai Barkai
CEO at CopilotKit
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Agent-User Interactions are now evolving from text exchanges to rich UIs. Until recently, most conversations looked like this:
User:
"Find me a holiday package to Bali in March."
Agent:
(six packages in prose, each with dates, hotel, flights, price)
User:
"The five-night one with breakfast."
Agent:
"Here's the link. You can book it on the operator's site."
Agents could plan the trip, but everything came back as walls of text. They had no standard way to render a selectable list of packages, a map of the destinations, or a date picker to carry you through the rest of the booking, inside the conversation itself.
Generative UI is the layer that lets agents build interfaces at runtime, shaped by what each request needs - giving users a rich, interactive experience. Implementing that takes two pieces: a way to describe the UI and an agentic stack that connects your agent to your application and renders that UI.
A2UI (Agent-to-UI)
is Google's framework-agnostic open standard for Generative UI. The agent describes an interface as data, and your application draws it with the components you already have. It's transport-agnostic by design.
CopilotKit
provides the agent-integration stack to integrate with agent frameworks like “LangChain”, “AWS Strands”, “Google ADK”, etc. for building user-facing agentic apps. It provides a toolkit for building rich applications with A2UI protocol, including the chat surface, runtime, and leverages A2UI renderer, across React and Angular. CopilotKit also provides custom A2UI renderers for Vue and Slack.
What is A2UI?
Generative UI covers a spectrum of approaches, from using predefined higher order components, to enabling your AI agent to have the flexibility to decide how to build the UI.
At the controlled end, you build each component ahead of time, and the agent picks which one to render and with what data. It's brand-safe but it does not allow for deep customization and personalization based on the user’s intent. At the open end, the agent returns a raw UI program written in HTML, Javascript and/or Dart that renders inside a sandboxed iframe. That covers anything you did not plan for, at the cost of a surface that drifts from your design system and executes code a model wrote.
A2UI
works through the entire spectrum. It participates in
controlled generation with decision models
like Typesafe’s Jev and also open-ended code generation that may output A2UI JSON messages. The declarative mode, where agents assemble pre-declared components and functions, is the most popular. A2UI is the framework-agnostic standard for declaring UI intent, so local or remote agents can generate your UI from your existing component catalog using a common language.
Security first.
A2UI is a declarative data format rather than executable code. The client keeps a catalog of trusted components, so anything the agent invents outside that set is caught before it reaches the screen.
LLM-friendly and streaming.
The payload is a flat list of small JSON messages that reference each other by ID, so the agent emits it incrementally and the client renders components as they arrive.
Framework-agnostic and portable.
The same response renders through
React, Lit, Angular, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose (Android) or Flutter
(multi-platform), and through
community renderers
for Vue, or even the terminal.
Frontend developers can now ship the building blocks once, and the agent composes them for each request.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
The
Basic Catalog
ships 18 general-purpose primitives across layout, display, input, and containers. The agent can compose entirely different interfaces from the same 18 primitives, depending on what the request needs.
The Basic Catalog is deliberately sparse, so most production apps
define their own custom catalog
. A custom component can be anything your frontend already renders, including a live map the agent fills with coordinates while your renderer draws the route.
How A2UI and CopilotKit work together
CopilotKit is built on
AG-UI (Agent-User Interaction Protocol)
, which supports A2UI payload and provides Agent SDKs across many agentic backends.
Your agent emits A2UI operations. AG-UI carries them to the client as typed events. When the user takes any action, the values are sent back along the same stream.
A2UI works with any AG-UI compatible agent.
Frameworks like Google ADK, LangChain, Mastra and Strands are all AG-UI compatible, so the setup is identical whichever one your agent runs on.
Setting up A2UI in your app
Setup comes down to two things: connecting your agent to CopilotKit, and defining which components the agent is allowed to use.
Using Google ADK as the example, the
ag_ui_adk
package wraps any ADK agent and serves it as an AG-UI endpoint on FastAPI:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from ag_ui_adk import ADKAgent, add_adk_fastapi_endpoint
root_agent = LlmAgent(
name="flight_agent",
model="gemini-3.8-flash",
instruction="Help users find and book flights. Call generate_a2ui to show results.",
)
adk_agent = ADKAgent(
adk_agent=root_agent,
app_name="flights",
user_id="demo_user",
use_in_memory_services=True,
)
app = FastAPI()
add_adk_fastapi_endpoint(app, adk_agent, path="/")
Python
Copied
On the app side, you register that endpoint with the CopilotKit runtime at
/api/copilotkit
. It's a few lines of standard setup, covered in the
Google ADK quickstart
, and it needs nothing A2UI-specific.
A2UI itself turns on from the client, where your components already are. Define what the agent is allowed to draw, map each definition to a renderer, and pass the catalog to the CopilotKit provider.
import { CopilotKit, CopilotChat } from '@copilotkit/react-core/v2';
import {
createCatalog,
type CatalogDefinitions,
type CatalogRenderers,
} from '@copilotkit/a2ui-renderer';
import { z } from 'zod';
const catalogDefinitions = {
FlightCard: {
description: 'A flight result with airline, times, and stops.',
props: z.object({
airline: z.string(),
departs: z.string(),
arrives: z.string(),
stops: z.number(),
}),
},
} satisfies CatalogDefinitions;
const catalogRenderers = {
FlightCard: MyFlightCard, // your React component
} satisfies CatalogRenderers<typeof catalogDefinitions>;
const catalog = createCatalog(catalogDefinitions, catalogRenderers, {
catalogId: 'flight-catalog',
includeBasicCatalog: true,
});
<CopilotKit runtimeUrl="/api/copilotkit" a2ui={{ catalog }}>
<CopilotChat />
</CopilotKit>
JavaScript
Copied
The
description
goes into the agent's prompt, so the model knows when to reach for
FlightCard
instead of a generic card. The Zod schema validates the props it sends back.
The A2UI configuration can be set up ahead of time on the server, or it can be created dynamically, shipped from the client to the server with the request. The ADK code above used dynamic configuration which is why it used generate_a2ui without defining it. The
docs
cover both approaches.
That’s the CopilotKit path. You can also consume the event stream directly with
@ag-ui/client
and hand the A2UI operations to any compliant renderer:
@a2ui/react
, or the Flutter, Lit, or Angular equivalent.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Building bi-directional A2UI surfaces
Most agent-generated UI is one-shot. The agent draws something, you read it, and it goes stale the moment anything changes.
A2UI surfaces are bi-directional and the components are reactive
, which makes multi-step flows possible. Any action the user takes on the interface (picking dates, choosing a flight, entering passenger details) travels back along the same stream, and the agent re-emits the surface from there using those values.
Here is a high-level architecture example of an end-to-end booking flow, with an AG-UI agent on Cloud Run streaming A2UI surfaces to a CopilotKit frontend.
Two things make the round trip work: inputs bound to a data path, and a button carrying an action that names which paths to send back.
{ "id": "cabin", "component": "ChoicePicker", "variant": "mutuallyExclusive",
"options": [ { "label": "Economy", "value": "eco" },
{ "label": "Business", "value": "biz" } ],
"value": { "path": "/booking/cabin" } },
{ "id": "confirm", "component": "Button", "child": "confirm_label",
"action": { "event": { "name": "confirmBooking",
"context": { "cabin": { "path": "/booking/cabin" },
"email": { "path": "/booking/email" } } } } }
JSON
Copied
Validation runs on the client, so a bad email shows an error inline without a model call. Nothing reaches the agent until the button fires.
Then the client sends the bound values, and the agent re-emits against the same
surfaceId
. That is how the whole flow lives on one surface: flight search, results, passenger details, and confirmation.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Benefits of running A2UI over AG-UI
Every AG-UI integration inherets these benefits, so you don't have to build them yourself:
Minimal server-side setup:
the catalog reaches the agent on setup, so registering it on the client is all it takes.
Generation in a dedicated sub-agent:
the catalog and protocol rules stay out of your main agent's context window, and the surface streams to the client as the sub-agent produces it.
Self-healing output:
invalid generations are caught and the specific errors go back for a correction, so nothing broken reaches the screen.
Graceful failure:
when retries are exhausted, the surface resolves to a short message and the conversation continues instead of dying in an error state.
Get Started
Create a complete A2UI + CopilotKit application. This creates a starter A2UI application with Copilotkit Agent integration.
npx copilotkit@latest create --name my-app --framework a2ui
Shell
Copied
The
CopilotKit Dojo
has runnable A2UI demos: fixed server-side schema, dynamic schema against a custom catalog, and an error-recovery example where an invalid first render heals into a valid one.
A2UI Composer
CopilotKit A2UI Docs
Use A2UI with Any Agent Framework & Harness
Explore how to build Generative UI Agents with
CopilotKit
, or dive into
A2UI documentation
to learn how to integrate A2UI with any framework of your choice.

items.title: Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation This post walks through the Agents CLI evaluation loop for systematically improving agent performance through continuous test
items.content:
Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation
- Google Developers Blog
Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation
OCT. 28, 2026
Pier Paolo Ippolito
Product Manager
Elia Secchi
Solutions Specialist
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
A live walkthrough of the Agents CLI eval loop, from a first run to regression tracking, model-backend experiments, and automated alerting
Introduction
Building an agent that works on a demo is a different problem from building an agent that stays working across model upgrades, tool changes, and new conversation shapes. The first takes a weekend; the second takes a loop. A team writes test cases, runs them, grades them, reads what failed, changes the agent, and runs the cases again. If the score goes up, the change was good. If it goes down, revert. Over weeks of this, the agent inches toward the ceiling of what the model, tools, and prompt can do together. The quality-engineering name for this is hill-climbing.
The Agents CLI eval namespace was built around this loop. The commands are small and framework-agnostic: eval generate runs the agent against a dataset of cases, eval grade scores the generated traces, eval compare diffs two run results side by side, eval analyze clusters failures into themes, and eval optimize runs an automated hill-climbing pass on the agent's prompt.
Below: baseline → regression → model swap → scheduling and alerting.
Setup
The scaffold used throughout is the LangChain template that ships with Agents CLI v1.8.0. The setup is a single command:
agents-cli create my-agent \
--agent google/agents-cli/extensions/langchain/template@v1.8.0 \
-d cloud_run
cd my-agent && agents-cli install
Plain text
Copied
The scaffold ships with an eval dataset at
tests/eval/datasets/basic-dataset.json,
a config at
tests/eval/eval_config.yaml
, and a custom LLM-as-judge metric at
tests/eval/response_quality.py
. The config declares the metric to run:
# tests/eval/eval_config.yaml
metrics_to_run:
- custom_response_quality
custom_metrics:
- name: custom_response_quality
custom_function_file: response_quality.py
Plain text
Copied
The metric grades each response on a 1-to-5 scale for accuracy, relevance, and clarity, using
gemini-3.8-flash
as the judge. The default dataset has a single trivial case, which is not enough for a hill-climb. The first thing we do is expand it to four cases that probe different behaviors:
{
"eval_cases": [
{"name": "greeting",
"agent_data": {"turns": [{"events": [{"author": "user", "content": {"parts": [{"text": "hello"}]}}]}]}},
{"name": "sf_weather",
"agent_data": {"turns": [{"events": [{"author": "user", "content": {"parts": [{"text": "What is the weather in San Francisco?"}]}}]}]}},
{"name": "rome_weather",
"agent_data": {"turns": [{"events": [{"author": "user", "content": {"parts": [{"text": "How is the weather in Rome today?"}]}}]}]}},
{"name": "off_topic",
"agent_data": {"turns": [{"events": [{"author": "user", "content": {"parts": [{"text": "Who won the 2024 World Series?"}]}}]}]}}
]
}
Plain text
Copied
Four cases: a greeting, a weather question the mock tool handles with the hardcoded foggy response, a weather question for a city the tool defaults on, and an off-topic question that the agent has to decide how to handle. This is a small dataset by design; the hill-climbing loop pays off when the dataset is small enough to run on every change.
Step 1: Running the First Eval
With the dataset in place, we
run eval generate
to drive the agent against each case, then
eval grade
to score the resulting traces:
agents-cli eval generate --dataset tests/eval/datasets/basic-dataset.json \
-o tests/eval/output/
agents-cli eval grade --traces tests/eval/output/eval_dataset_*.json \
--config tests/eval/eval_config.yaml
Plain text
Copied
The baseline run produces:
Evaluation Summary
custom_response_quality:
num_cases_total: 4
num_cases_valid: 4
num_cases_error: 0
mean_score: 4.0000
stdev_score: 1.4142
Saved full results to artifacts/grade_results/results_20261003_224516.json
Saved HTML results to artifacts/grade_results/results_20261003_224516.html
Plain text
Copied
Mean 4.0 out of 5 across four cases, with a standard deviation of 1.41. That stdev tells us immediately that the cases are not scoring uniformly, which is a healthier starting point than a flat 5.0 across the board. A flat 5.0 either means the agent is perfect (unlikely) or the dataset is too easy to show variation. 4.0 with real spread is a hill to climb.
Step 2: Making a Change and Re-Running
To demonstrate the loop, we introduce a realistic regression. A developer working across several agent projects accidentally pastes the wrong system prompt into our weather agent: a chef persona meant for a different codebase. In
app/agent.py
:
# Before
root_agent: CompiledStateGraph = create_agent(
model=llm, tools=[get_weather], system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant"
)
# After
root_agent: CompiledStateGraph = create_agent(
model=llm, tools=[get_weather],
system_prompt=(
"You are a professional chef. Help users with recipes, cooking "
"techniques, and ingredient substitutions. Always suggest a recipe "
"at the end of every response."
),
)
Plain text
Copied
The change compiles, the agent still runs, and nothing in the pre-eval pipeline (lint, unit tests, type checks) catches it. Re-running the same eval generate plus eval grade sequence produces:
Evaluation Summary
custom_response_quality:
num_cases_total: 4
num_cases_valid: 4
num_cases_error: 0
mean_score: 2.7500
stdev_score: 0.9574
Saved full results to artifacts/grade_results/results_20261003_225158.json
JSON
Copied
Mean 2.75, down from 4.0. The judge agrees with our intuition that a chef persona on a weather agent is a worse product than a general-purpose helpful assistant. The stdev also tightened from 1.41 to 0.96, consistent with the chef prompt pushing most cases toward the same mediocre range.
A 1.25-point drop on a 1-to-5 scale is substantial, and the kind of regression that can slip through code review when the diff looks small ("one string literal changed"). The loop surfaced the change at all, with a specific number attached to it, before the agent reached production.
Step 3: Comparing Two Runs
Mean scores are a start; the per-case diff is where the hill-climb happens. eval compare reads two result files and produces a structured JSON diff:
agents-cli eval compare \
artifacts/grade_results/results_20261003_224516.json \
artifacts/grade_results/results_20261003_225158.json
JSON
Copied
The output lists which keys changed and which stayed the same:
{
"baseline_keys": ["agent_info", "eval_case_results", "evaluation_dataset",
"metadata", "summary_metrics", "win_rates"],
"candidate_keys": ["agent_info", "eval_case_results", "evaluation_dataset",
"metadata", "summary_metrics", "win_rates"],
"changed_keys": ["eval_case_results", "metadata.creation_timestamp"],
"unchanged_keys": ["agent_info", "evaluation_dataset", "metadata",
"summary_metrics", "win_rates"],
"differences": { ... per-case score diffs ... }
}
JSON
Copied
The
differences
object has the full per-case breakdown with the baseline and candidate values side by side. For a hill-climbing workflow, we typically pipe the output through
jq
or a small Python script to extract the signal; the raw JSON is the complete evidence.
Step 4: Reading the Per-Case Scores
Walking the two result files and lining up the scores per case shows where the regression landed:
case                  baseline → candidate   what the chef prompt did
greeting              5.0 → 4.0  ↓          launched into an unsolicited recipe pitch after "hello"
sf_weather            4.0 → 2.0  ↓          ignored the weather tool, hallucinated conditions
rome_weather          2.0 → 2.0  ·          already hallucinated at baseline; chef persona did not make it worse
off_topic             5.0 → 3.0  ↓          answered the Dodgers question but tacked on a recipe
Plain text
Copied
Three cases dropped, one held. The most important of the three is
sf_weather
: the chef persona pulled the model's attention away from the registered
get_weather
tool, so the agent stopped calling it and started making up weather values. Unit tests can't catch this: the code runs, the tool is still registered, but the model's behavior around it has shifted. Only an end-to-end eval that scores the response in context surfaces this.
The mean drop by itself (−1.25) is a clear signal, but the per-case breakdown is what tells the developer where to look. A one-line system-prompt change propagated through three different cases in three different ways: greeting lost a point on tone,
sf_weather
lost two on tool usage,
off_topic
lost two on scope creep.
Step 5: Swapping the Model Backend
A common hill-climbing question is whether a cheaper or faster model would do the job acceptably. For the LangChain template, the model is defined in
app/agent.py
:
LLM = "gemini-3.8-flash"
llm = ChatGoogleGenerativeAI(model=LLM, temperature=0)
Plain text
Copied
We swap
gemini-3.8-flash
for
gemini-2.5-flash
(restoring the helpful system prompt first), re-run
eval generate
plus
eval grade
, and compare the two result files. The mean drops from 4.00 to 2.75, the same magnitude as the chef-prompt regression, but the per-case breakdown tells a completely different story:
case                  3.8-flash → 2.5-flash
greeting              5.0 → 5.0  ·
sf_weather            4.0 → 3.0  ↓
rome_weather          2.0 → 2.0  ·
off_topic             5.0 → 1.0  ↓↓
Plain text
Copied
The cheaper model matched 3.8-flash exactly on the greeting and rome_weather cases and lost a point on sf_weather (slightly less polished phrasing). The whole visible drop traces to
off_topic
, where the cheaper model refused with a hedge about the event "not having happened yet" (a training-cutoff artifact), and the judge marked it harshly.
The lesson is that the summary number is misleading. Look only at the mean and you'd call
gemini-2.5-flash
as bad as the chef prompt. Look at the per-case breakdown and you'd call it a reasonable swap for most of the agent's workload, with one case (handling out-of-scope questions about recent events) exposing a real limitation. If the production distribution of user questions matches the first three cases more than the fourth, the swap is worth considering. If
off_topic
-style questions are common, it is not.
Two caveats on this experiment. First, model swaps interact with the prompt: a prompt tuned for a stronger model often leaks capability when ported to a weaker one, so the right comparison is "weaker model with a prompt tuned for it" versus "stronger model with its own tuned prompt." Second, the Vertex AI Eval Service calls a judge model to grade the traces, and the judge is held constant across the comparison. Changing the judge is a different experiment and should be done separately.
Step 6: Scheduling the Loop
Agents CLI does not ship a scheduler, but the
eval
commands are designed to drop into standard infrastructure. The pattern we can use here is a cron job or Cloud Scheduler trigger that runs
eval generate
plus
eval grade
on a cadence and writes the results to a persistent location:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/scheduled_eval.sh — invoked nightly by cron or Cloud Scheduler
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
DATE=$(date +%Y%m%d)
OUT=artifacts/scheduled_runs/$DATE
mkdir -p $OUT
agents-cli eval generate --dataset tests/eval/datasets/regression.json -o $OUT/
agents-cli eval grade --traces $OUT/eval_dataset_*.json \
--config tests/eval/eval_config.yaml \
--output $OUT/
Plain text
Copied
A nightly run against a stable regression dataset catches drift from model updates, data changes in the agent's tools, and dependencies that shift under the agent's feet. For a production agent, the scheduled run also captures the model vendor's quiet upgrades, which can move the agent's behavior without any change on our side. The dataset for the scheduled run is typically larger than the one used in the inner loop (dozens to hundreds of cases rather than a few), since it only runs once a day.
Step 7: Alerting on Score Drops
The scheduled run produces a result file every day, but a file nobody looks at is not an alert. The pattern here can be a wrapper script that compares each new run's mean against a baseline (the previous run, or a committed known-good) and exits non-zero when the drop exceeds a threshold. The non-zero exit is what triggers the alert from the surrounding scheduler.
Here is an example:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Exit non-zero if an eval result dips below baseline by more than --threshold."""
